pages.text: On her first night at boarding school, Patience sat on a metal bed in a long dormitory full of strangers. Beside her stood a wooden chop box her mother had packed: gari, sugar, tinned milk, a tin of sardines and a bag of groundnuts. The room was noisy. Girls shouted, buckets clanged, and a radio played somewhere. Patience swallowed hard. She missed her mother’s kitchen.

The room was noisy.
Girls shouted, buckets clanged, and a radio played somewhere.
Patience swallowed hard.
She missed her mother’s kitchen.
pages.alt: A girl sits on a bunk beside a wooden chop box in a busy dormitory.

pages.text: The bell rang for prep, then for supper, then for lights out. Supper was a scoop of beans and a slice of bread. Patience ate half of it. At nine o’clock, Madam Dankyi, the house mistress, walked down the aisle with her keys. “Lights out, ladies,” she said. “Rest well. Tomorrow is a long day.” Then the dormitory went dark, and Patience’s eyes filled with tears.

pages.alt: A house mistress walks between rows of bunk beds as the lights go out.

pages.text: A small torch clicked on above her. Eunice, a senior, leaned down from the next bunk. “First night?” she whispered. Patience nodded. “Everyone cries on the first night,” said Eunice. “I did. It does not mean you are weak. It means you love your home.” Patience let out a small laugh and wiped her face.

pages.alt: A senior girl leans from a top bunk with a small torch, speaking softly to a younger girl.

pages.text: “Do you have a chop box?” asked Eunice. Patience pointed. “Good,” said Eunice. “In this house, a chop box is a treasure, but it is also a gift to share. Tomorrow night, we will have a little feast, if you want.” She opened her tin of biscuits and passed one down. “Welcome to Red Wing,” she whispered. “You are not alone here.”

pages.text: The next evening, six girls sat in a circle on the dormitory floor with their chop boxes. Patience added gari, sugar and groundnuts to a big bowl. Another girl added milk. Another added sardines and pepper. They mixed it and ate with spoons, laughing quietly. “A feast!” said Eunice. “Everyone brings a little, and everyone has plenty.” Patience ate until her tummy was full.

pages.text: Madam Dankyi explained the dormitory rules the next day. “Keep your space tidy. Do not borrow without asking. Do not take food that is not yours. Be quiet after lights out. And look after each other.” She looked at Patience kindly. “If you are ever unwell, sad or frightened, tell me or a senior. That is what we are here for.” Patience felt safe.

pages.text: That weekend, Patience wrote home, with her address and the date at the top. “Red Wing, Hillcrest Girls’ Boarding School, Koforidua. 20th February, 2027. Dear Mother, I hope you are well. I miss you very much, but I am settling in. A kind senior called Eunice has helped me, and I have made new friends. Thank you for the chop box. We shared it, and it was delicious. Please greet Father and my brothers for me. I will write again next week. Your loving daughter, Patience.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: Patience wrote that she misses her mother in full, honest words. She did not use a chat shortcut such as “mis u”. Short, warm sentences with clear details make a letter easy to read. Letters can show feelings, and exam letters should show them in complete words. The end.
